newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Brierley says battling against history.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Brierley says battling against history.

text.p: Brierley Investments Ltd chairman Bob Matthew said on Wednesday the New Zealand investment company was fighting history when it grappled with shareholder dissent about performance.
BIL last week had to deal with shareholders in surly mood at the annual meeting, including founder president Sir Ron Brierley who bemoaned the performance of the BIL share price.

Matthew told Reuters many shareholders fondly recall the heady days in 1987 when the share price was over NZ$5 (US3.55) against NZ$1.27 today, but they forget the company was then capitalised at an unsustainable three to four times asset backing.
Matthew said the mood of the shareholders has actually improved.
"I would say there is far less angst than there was in the early 1990s," he said.
He attributes a considerable part of the problem to BIL's high dividend policy -- it pays nine cents per share a year.
"The perception is that that constitutes 'my interest, not my return'," Matthew said.
He estimates BIL enhanced its value by NZ$600-700 million in 1995/96, of which a third was via dividend payments.

Despite the negative attitude of some shareholders, and a view from Matthew himself that, given accumulated tax losses it may be more advantageous from a tax point of view to have a lower payout, BIL is not about to change dividend policy. International and local institutions and many long-standing shareholders want the high dividends.
"We are going to maintain the dividend at its present levels and we have got no point in the future set where we would reduce it."
Some shareholders tackled BIL on a lack of clear strategy, with at least one suggesting BIL should quit its loss-making U.S. investments.

Matthew said BIL wanted to concentrate as an Australasian investment company but with interest in Asia. However, he did not rule out new investments in Britain despite a bad experience with British hotels group Thistle.

BIL had built an appreciation of that market "and traditionally found, with at least one notable exception, that it is possible to acquire businesses that could be much better run that they presently are".
Some companies in Britain were extraordinarily inadequately run, he said. However BIL, which still has 46 percent of recently listed Thistle, will not increase its overall exposure to Britain.
Matthew said while the board is agreed on a progressive withdrawal, it doesn't favour a fire sale.
"There are some people who have the luxury of ignoring when it is the most profitable time to do things," he said.

Matthew is bullish about BIL exploiting the relationship with its 20 percent shareholder, the Delham consortium -- Hong Leong Group Malaysia, Sembawang Corp of Singapore, Salim Group of Indonesia and Haw Par Brothers and Hong Leong of Singapore.
While analysts are getting impatient for an announcement of tangible action, Matthew is quietly confident.
"We have collectively agreed on what we want to do and how we go about it but opportunities are not simply picked up out of the gutter."
Any move the group makes will be "substantial".

Although Delham, whose stake is held via Malex Industries of Malaysia, has yet to nominate anyone for the BIL board, there have been numerous meetings at executive level and a number of projects are on the boil at a subsidiary level, Matthew said.

"It's a cordial relationship. We both have a common theme, we can both see the nexus between Australasia and Asia, but it is the opportunities for exploiting the productive or creative capacity of Australasia we want to explore," he said.
